What does this imply about convergent versus divergent evolution, and why is cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone insufficient evidence of homology?"}

item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"The occurrence of NAD(P)-binding enzymes in multiple SCOP folds shows that NAD(P) recognition evolved independently more than once: similar cofactor-binding features can be convergent adaptations to the same chemical and geometric constraints. Divergent evolution is supported only within groups having stronger evidence of common ancestry—typically a SCOP family or superfamily with a conserved structural core and compatible sequence/mechanistic evidence. A shared fold alone is weaker and may reflect only a common architecture.\n\nCofactor binding is therefore not a homology marker by itself. Glycine-rich loops, βα motifs, phosphate/ribose contacts, and even similar catalytic residues can arise independently or occupy non-equivalent positions in different topologies. Conversely, homologs may diverge in cofactor specificity or active-site residues. Homology claims require concordant evidence such as global topology and residue correspondence, statistically significant sequence/profile similarity, conserved core packing, mechanistic context, and phylogenetic consistency. Function or substrate specificity should not be transferred solely from NAD(P) binding or local active-site resemblance, and a structural template from another fold—or a remote member sharing only the fold—may be unsuitable for detailed modeling. Representatives should be chosen from the closest supported family/superfamily rather than merely from any NAD(P)-binding protein.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
